name: Setup: dev environment
title: Setup: your dev environment
thesis: Install Python 3.12, Git, VS Code, a virtual environment and (optionally) Docker, then prove it all works with a tested hello_fde.py checker. An FDE sets up environments on unfamiliar machines constantly, so doing it cleanly and verifiably is a core habit.

project.tree:
p0-setup/
  README.md
  requirements.txt
  .env.example
  .gitignore
  hello_fde.py
  tests/
    conftest.py
    test_hello_fde.py

setup.title: Install Python 3.12
setup.body: Python runs every project in this module. Install 3.12 and confirm the version. On Windows, tick 'Add python.exe to PATH' if you use the python.org installer; the py launcher lets you pick a version.
setup.code:
# Windows (PowerShell)
winget install Python.Python.3.12
py -3.12 --version

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install python@3.12
python3.12 --version

# Linux (Debian/Ubuntu; older releases may need pyenv or the deadsnakes PPA)
sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3.12 python3.12-venv
python3.12 --version

setup.title: Install Git and introduce yourself
setup.body: Git tracks every change you make. Set your name and email once so your commits are labeled.
setup.code:
# Windows
winget install Git.Git
# macOS
brew install git
# Linux
sudo apt install git

# all platforms
git --version
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

setup.title: Install VS Code and the Python extension
setup.body: VS Code is the editor used throughout. Install the Python extension from Microsoft so you get linting, debugging and a test runner. On macOS, run 'Shell Command: Install code command in PATH' from the command palette so the checker can find it.
setup.code:
# Windows
winget install Microsoft.VisualStudioCode
# macOS
brew install --cask visual-studio-code
# Linux: download the .deb or .rpm from code.visualstudio.com, then
sudo apt install ./code_*.deb

# all platforms
code --install-extension ms-python.python
code --version

setup.title: Install Docker Desktop (optional)
setup.body: Later projects use Docker for Postgres, but each one has a no-Docker fallback, so you can skip this for now.
setup.code:
# Windows
winget install Docker.DockerDesktop
# macOS
brew install --cask docker
# Linux
sudo apt install docker.io && sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

docker --version

setup.title: Create the project and a virtual environment
setup.body: A virtual environment is a private folder of packages for one project, so projects never fight over versions. Activate it every time you open a new terminal; your prompt shows (.venv) when it is active.
setup.code:
# macOS / Linux
mkdir p0-setup && cd p0-setup
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Windows PowerShell
mkdir p0-setup; cd p0-setup
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
# if activation is blocked, run once:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned

setup.title: Put API keys in .env, never in code
setup.body: Copy .env.example to .env and paste your real key there. python-dotenv loads it into environment variables at runtime, and .gitignore keeps .env out of Git. A key is optional for this project.
setup.code:
# macOS / Linux
cp .env.example .env
# Windows PowerShell
copy .env.example .env

steps.title: Pin the dependencies
steps.body: Only two packages: python-dotenv to read .env files and pytest to run tests. The >= bounds say 'at least this version' so pip can pick a recent compatible one.

steps.title: Describe secrets without storing them
steps.body:
.env.example is committed to Git so teammates know which variables exist. It holds placeholders only.

The real .env stays on your machine.
steps.code:
# Copy this file to .env and fill in real values. Never commit .env.
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here

steps.title: Keep junk and secrets out of Git
steps.body: Ignore the virtual environment, Python caches and .env. Doing this on day one prevents the most common beginner leak: an API key pushed to GitHub.

steps.title: Write the checker
steps.body:
Each check is a small function that returns a CheckResult (name, ok, detail, required). check_tool finds a command with shutil.which, runs it with --version and parses the number with a regular expression.

Notice that which and runner are parameters with real defaults. Tests can pass in fakes, so they never depend on what is installed on the test machine. mask() makes sure an API key is never printed in full.

steps.title: Let tests import the project
steps.body: pytest runs from the project folder, but this small conftest.py makes the import of hello_fde work no matter where pytest is started.
steps.code:
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# Let tests import modules from the project root.
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

steps.title: Test the checker functions
steps.body: The tests cover version parsing, a too-old Python, a missing tool, a fake tool output, a tool that hangs, venv detection and key masking. None of them run a real command, so they pass on any machine in under a second.
steps.code:
import subprocess
from types import SimpleNamespace

import hello_fde as h


def test_parse_version_finds_numbers():
    assert h.parse_version("git version 2.43.0") == "2.43.0"
    assert h.parse_version("Docker version 27.1.1, build 6312585") == "27.1.1"
    assert h.parse_version("1.95.3\nabc123\nx64") == "1.95.3"
    assert h.parse_version("no digits here") is None
    assert h.parse_version(None) is None


def test_check_python_passes_and_fails():
    assert h.check_python((3, 12), version_info=(3, 12, 4)).ok
    old = h.check_python((3, 12), version_info=(3, 9, 1))
    assert not old.ok
    assert "need 3.12+" in old.detail


def test_check_tool_missing():
    result = h.check_tool("git", which=lambda name: None)
    assert not result.ok
    assert result.detail == "not found on PATH"


def test_check_tool_parses_fake_output():
    def fake_runner(cmd, **kwargs):
        return SimpleNamespace(stdout="git version 2.45.1\n", stderr="")

    result = h.check_tool("git", which=lambda n: "/usr/bin/git", runner=fake_runner)
    assert result.ok
    assert result.detail == "2.45.1"


def test_check_tool_handles_crash():
    def broken_runner(cmd, **kwargs):
        raise subprocess.TimeoutExpired(cmd, 15)

    result = h.check_tool("docker", required=False,
                          which=lambda n: "/usr/bin/docker", runner=broken_runner)
    assert not result.ok and not result.required
    assert "failed to run" in result.detail


def test_check_venv():
    assert h.check_venv(prefix="/proj/.venv", base_prefix="/usr").ok
    assert not h.check_venv(prefix="/usr", base_prefix="/usr").ok


def test_env_key_is_masked():
    result = h.check_env_key("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", env={"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY": "sk-ant-abcdef123456"})
    assert result.ok
    assert "abcdef123456" not in result.detail
    missing = h.check_env_key("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", env={})
    assert not missing.ok and not missing.required


def test_format_result_tags():
    assert h.format_result(h.CheckResult("git", True, "2.4")).startswith("[OK  ]")
    assert h.format_result(h.CheckResult("git", False, "x")).startswith("[FAIL]")
    assert h.format_result(h.CheckResult("docker", False, "x", required=False)).startswith("[WARN]")

project.interview: I built a small environment checker I run on any new machine or customer VM before starting work. Each check is a pure function with injectable dependencies, so the tests use fakes and run anywhere. The trade-offs: I only verify that a tool exists and reports a version, not that it is fully configured, and I mask secrets rather than printing them because terminal output often ends up in screenshots and tickets.

ideas: One virtual environment per project keeps package versions from colliding
Secrets live in environment variables loaded from an untracked .env file, with a committed .env.example as documentation
Passing dependencies like which and runner as parameters makes code testable without mocking libraries
A checker script turns 'works on my machine' into a repeatable, one-command answer
traps: Forgetting to activate the virtual environment, so pip installs into the system Python and imports fail later
Committing .env or pasting a key into source code; once it is in Git history, rotate the key
Having several Pythons on PATH and not knowing which one 'python' runs; check with python --version and where python (Windows) or which python
qa: Why use a virtual environment instead of installing packages globally?

Each project gets its own isolated set of packages and versions, so upgrading one project cannot break another, and requirements.txt describes exactly what that project needs. It also avoids needing admin rights and keeps the system Python clean.
How do you handle API keys in a project you share with a customer?

Keep them out of code and Git: read them from environment variables, load local ones from an ignored .env file, commit only a .env.example with placeholders, and never log them in full. In production use the platform's secret manager, and rotate any key that was ever exposed.

thesis: Build a command-line tool that turns a messy customer CSV into clean.csv plus a rejects.csv that explains every dropped row. Cleaning a customer's data export is often the first real task on an FDE engagement, and explaining the rejects is what earns trust.

    clean.csv
    rejects.csv

    conftest.py
    test_cleaner.py

setup.title: Create the folder and virtual environment
setup.body: Same routine as Project 0: a fresh folder, a fresh virtual environment, then install pytest.
setup.code:
# macOS / Linux
mkdir -p p1-csv-cleaner/tests && cd p1-csv-cleaner
python3 -m venv .venv

steps.title: Dependencies and ignores
steps.body: Only pytest is needed; everything else is the standard library. The output folder is ignored because it is regenerated on every run.

steps.title: Generate a messy sample file
steps.body:
Never practise on real customer data. This script builds 20 good fake customers with a fixed random seed, then appends hand-written problem rows: missing and invalid emails, impossible and future dates, a bad country code, a non-numeric id, duplicate ids and a duplicate email hidden by different casing.

Because the seed is fixed, everyone gets the same file and the tests can assert exact counts.
steps.code:
"""make_sample.py: generate a small, fake, messy customer CSV for practice.

All names are invented. The same seed always gives the same file.
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

FIRST = ["Ana", "Ben", "Chen", "Dara", "Eli", "Fatima", "Goran", "Hana", "Ivan", "Juno"]
LAST = ["Silva", "Okafor", "Li", "Novak", "Haddad", "Kim", "Moreau", "Patel"]
COUNTRIES = ["US", "GB", "IN", "DE", "BR", "JP"]
FIELDS = ["customer_id", "name", "email", "signup_date", "country"]

# Hand-written problem rows, so every rule in cleaner.py gets exercised.
MESSY_ROWS = [
    ["21", "  Rosa   Diaz ", " ROSA.DIAZ@Example.COM ", "2024/03/05", "us"],  # fixable
    ["22", "Omar Farouk", "", "2024-02-11", "EG"],                            # missing email
    ["23", "Lena Berg", "lena.berg(at)example.com", "2024-01-20", "SE"],      # invalid email
    ["24", "Tom Reyes", "tom.reyes@example.com", "31/02/2024", "MX"],        # impossible date
    ["25", "Mia Wong", "mia.wong@example.com", "yesterday", "SG"],           # not a date
    ["26", "Kai Lund", "kai.lund@example.com", "2099-01-01", "NO"],          # future date
    ["27", "", "noname@example.com", "2024-04-02", "US"],                    # missing name
    ["28", "Zoe Adams", "zoe.adams@example.com", "2024-05-06", "USA"],       # bad country
    ["abc", "Sam Cole", "sam.cole@example.com", "2024-05-07", "CA"],         # bad id
    ["3", "Duplicate Id", "dup.id@example.com", "2024-05-08", "US"],         # duplicate id
    ["29", "Rosa Diaz", "rosa.diaz@example.com", "2024-03-05", "US"],        # duplicate email
    ["30", "Ivy Nash", "ivy.nash@example.com", "05 Jun 2024", "gb"],         # fixable
]


def make_rows(n=20, seed=42):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    rows = []
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        first, last = rng.choice(FIRST), rng.choice(LAST)
        signup = date(2023, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=rng.randint(0, 540))
        email = f"{first}.{last}{i}@example.com".lower()
        rows.append([str(i), f"{first} {last}", email, signup.isoformat(), rng.choice(COUNTRIES)])
    rows.extend(MESSY_ROWS)
    rows.append(list(rows[6]))  # an exact duplicate of customer 7
    return rows


def write_sample(path="data/customers_messy.csv", n=20, seed=42):
    path = Path(path)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with path.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow(FIELDS)
        writer.writerows(make_rows(n, seed))
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = write_sample()
    print(f"Wrote {out}")

steps.title: Write the validation rules
steps.body:
clean_row trims every field, then checks one rule at a time and raises RowError on the first problem. RowError carries a short kind (for the summary) and a detail (for the rejects file).

Dates accept only unambiguous formats. 03/04/2024 could be March or April, so guessing would silently corrupt data; rejecting it is safer. The optional today argument lets tests freeze the calendar.

steps.title: Detect duplicates and keep line numbers
steps.body: Duplicates are checked after cleaning, so ' ROSA.DIAZ@Example.COM ' and 'rosa.diaz@example.com' count as the same person. The first occurrence wins, and each reject records its original line number (line 1 is the header) so a customer can find it in their own file.

steps.title: Add file handling and the command line
steps.body: run reads the input (utf-8-sig handles files saved by Excel), refuses files missing required columns, and writes both outputs. main uses argparse, so --help works for free and a missing file gives a clean usage error with exit code 2 instead of a stack trace.
steps.code:
def write_csv(path, rows, fields):
    with open(path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields)
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)


def run(input_path, out_dir, today=None):
    with open(input_path, newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        missing = [c for c in FIELDS if c not in (reader.fieldnames or [])]
        if missing:
            raise SystemExit(f"error: input is missing columns: {', '.join(missing)}")
        rows = list(reader)
    clean, rejects = clean_rows(rows, today)
    out_dir = Path(out_dir)
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    write_csv(out_dir / "clean.csv", clean, FIELDS)
    write_csv(out_dir / "rejects.csv", rejects, ["line", *FIELDS, "kind", "reason"])
    return len(rows), clean, rejects


def main(argv=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Clean a messy customer CSV.")
    parser.add_argument("input", help="path to the messy CSV")
    parser.add_argument("--out-dir", default="output", help="folder for clean.csv and rejects.csv")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    if not Path(args.input).is_file():
        parser.error(f"file not found: {args.input}")

    total, clean, rejects = run(args.input, args.out_dir)
    print(f"Read {total} rows from {args.input}")
    print(f"  clean:   {len(clean):>3}  -> {Path(args.out_dir) / 'clean.csv'}")
    print(f"  rejects: {len(rejects):>3}  -> {Path(args.out_dir) / 'rejects.csv'}")
    if rejects:
        print("Reject reasons:")
        for kind, count in Counter(r["kind"] for r in rejects).most_common():
            print(f"  {kind:<16} {count}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

steps.title: Test the rules and the whole flow
steps.body: conftest.py adds the project folder to the import path (same file as Project 0). The parametrized test checks every rejection kind in one table. The end-to-end test generates the sample into a temporary folder, runs main and checks both output files and the printed summary.
steps.code:
# tests/conftest.py
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# Let tests import modules from the project root.
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))

# tests/test_cleaner.py
import csv
from datetime import date

import pytest

import cleaner
from make_sample import write_sample

TODAY = date(2025, 1, 1)  # fixed "today" so tests never depend on the calendar


def good(**overrides):
    row = {"customer_id": "1", "name": "Ana Silva", "email": "ana@example.com",
           "signup_date": "2024-03-05", "country": "us"}
    row.update(overrides)
    return row


def test_clean_row_normalizes_values():
    row = cleaner.clean_row(good(customer_id="007", name="  Ana   Silva ",
                                 email=" ANA@Example.COM ", signup_date="2024/03/05"), TODAY)
    assert row == {"customer_id": "7", "name": "Ana Silva", "email": "ana@example.com",
                   "signup_date": "2024-03-05", "country": "US"}


@pytest.mark.parametrize("field,value,kind", [
    ("email", "", "missing email"),
    ("email", "ana(at)example.com", "invalid email"),
    ("signup_date", "31/02/2024", "bad date"),
    ("signup_date", "yesterday", "bad date"),
    ("signup_date", "2030-01-01", "future date"),
    ("name", "   ", "missing name"),
    ("country", "USA", "bad country"),
    ("customer_id", "abc", "bad id"),
])
def test_clean_row_rejects(field, value, kind):
    with pytest.raises(cleaner.RowError) as err:
        cleaner.clean_row(good(**{field: value}), TODAY)
    assert err.value.kind == kind


def test_duplicates_keep_first_and_report_line():
    rows = [good(), good(customer_id="1", email="other@example.com"),
            good(customer_id="2", email="ANA@example.com")]
    clean, rejects = cleaner.clean_rows(rows, TODAY)
    assert len(clean) == 1
    assert [r["kind"] for r in rejects] == ["duplicate id", "duplicate email"]
    assert rejects[0]["line"] == 3
    assert "first seen on line 2" in rejects[0]["reason"]


def test_invalid_row_does_not_block_a_later_valid_one():
    rows = [good(email=""), good(email="ana@example.com")]
    clean, rejects = cleaner.clean_rows(rows, TODAY)
    assert len(clean) == 1 and len(rejects) == 1


def test_end_to_end_on_sample(tmp_path, capsys):
    src = write_sample(tmp_path / "messy.csv")
    out = tmp_path / "out"
    assert cleaner.main([str(src), "--out-dir", str(out)]) == 0

    with open(out / "clean.csv", newline="") as f:
        clean = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    with open(out / "rejects.csv", newline="") as f:
        rejects = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    assert len(clean) == 22
    assert len(rejects) == 11
    assert all(r["reason"] for r in rejects)
    assert len({r["email"] for r in clean}) == len(clean)  # no duplicate emails survive
    assert "Read 33 rows" in capsys.readouterr().out


def test_missing_columns_is_a_clear_error(tmp_path):
    bad = tmp_path / "bad.csv"
    bad.write_text("id,name\n1,Ana\n")
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit) as exc:
        cleaner.run(bad, tmp_path / "out")
    assert "missing columns" in str(exc.value)


def test_missing_file_exits_with_usage_error(tmp_path):
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit) as exc:
        cleaner.main([str(tmp_path / "nope.csv")])
    assert exc.value.code == 2

stretch: Add --strict so the tool exits with code 1 when any row is rejected, for use in a pipeline
Support DD/MM/YYYY behind an explicit --day-first flag instead of guessing
Stream rows instead of loading the whole file and time it on 1 million generated rows
Rewrite the rules with pydantic and compare readability and speed
project.interview: I built a CSV cleaner that splits a customer export into clean rows and rejects, where every reject keeps its original line number and a plain reason. The key trade-offs: I reject ambiguous dates instead of guessing, which is safer but needs a conversation with the customer; I keep the first duplicate, which is simple but may not be the most recent record; and I load the whole file into memory, which is fine for thousands of rows but would need streaming for millions.

ideas: Never drop bad rows silently: write them to a rejects file with a reason the customer can act on
Normalize first (trim, lowercase, collapse spaces), then deduplicate, or near-duplicates slip through
Accept only unambiguous formats; a wrong guess is worse than a visible rejection
A fixed-seed sample generator gives you realistic, repeatable test data with no privacy risk
traps: Parsing dates like 03/04/2024 without knowing the source convention, which swaps months and days silently
Checking duplicates on raw values, so case or whitespace differences hide the same customer
Writing tests that depend on today's date; pass 'today' in as a parameter
qa: A customer says your cleaner dropped 11 rows. How do you respond?

Point them to rejects.csv: each row has its original line number, a category and a specific reason, and the summary groups the counts. Then agree on rules for the gray areas, like which date format their system exports or which duplicate record should win, and turn those decisions into tests.
Why raise an exception per row instead of returning True or False?

The exception carries the reason, so the caller gets both the verdict and an explanation from one place. Catching RowError in one loop keeps the flow simple, and a separate kind field makes grouping for the summary easy without parsing message text.

name: Project 2: SQL analytics

thesis: Load the cleaned customers plus orders and order items into SQLite, answer business questions with 8 SQL queries including window functions, and catch a fan-out bug that inflates revenue. FDEs are asked 'what does the data say?' in their first week, and a wrong number from a bad join destroys credibility fast.

setup.title: Bring in the cleaned customers
setup.body: Copy Project 1's output so this project stands on its own. Then create the two order files from the next step.

steps.title: Create the order data
steps.body:
orders.csv has one row per order with an order-level total. order_items.csv has one row per product line, so one order can have several item rows. That one-to-many relationship is exactly what causes the fan-out bug later.

The data is small on purpose: 12 orders and 19 items, so you can check every answer by hand. Completed revenue adds up to 485.

steps.title: Define the schema and loader
steps.body:
The schema uses primary keys, foreign keys (SQLite only enforces them after PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON), a UNIQUE email and a CHECK on status, so bad data fails loudly at load time.

All inserts run in one transaction: either every table loads or none does. Values are always passed as ? parameters, never pasted into the SQL string. The default database is :memory:, which makes tests fast and isolated. requirements.txt contains only pytest>=8.0, and .gitignore adds *.db.
steps.code:
"""load_db.py: build a SQLite database from the CSV files in data/.

Usage:  python load_db.py --db shop.db [--customers ../p1-csv-cleaner/output/clean.csv]
"""
import argparse
import csv
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

DATA_DIR = Path(__file__).parent / "data"

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    email       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    signup_date TEXT NOT NULL,          -- ISO date, YYYY-MM-DD
    country     TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    order_date  TEXT NOT NULL,
    status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('completed', 'pending', 'refunded')),
    total       REAL NOT NULL           -- order-level amount: one value per order
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    product     TEXT NOT NULL,
    qty         INTEGER NOT NULL,
    unit_price  REAL NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_items_order ON order_items(order_id);
"""


def read_csv(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return list(csv.DictReader(f))


def insert_rows(conn, table, rows):
    if not rows:
        return 0
    cols = list(rows[0].keys())
    sql = f"INSERT INTO {table} ({', '.join(cols)}) VALUES ({', '.join('?' for _ in cols)})"
    conn.executemany(sql, [tuple(r[c] for c in cols) for r in rows])
    return len(rows)


def build_db(db_path=":memory:", customers_csv=None, data_dir=DATA_DIR):
    """Create the tables and load the CSVs. Returns an open connection."""
    data_dir = Path(data_dir)
    if db_path != ":memory:":
        Path(db_path).unlink(missing_ok=True)  # always rebuild from scratch
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    conn.executescript(SCHEMA)
    with conn:  # one transaction: all tables load, or none do
        insert_rows(conn, "customers", read_csv(customers_csv or data_dir / "customers.csv"))
        insert_rows(conn, "orders", read_csv(data_dir / "orders.csv"))
        insert_rows(conn, "order_items", read_csv(data_dir / "order_items.csv"))
    return conn


def main(argv=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Load CSVs into SQLite.")
    parser.add_argument("--db", default="shop.db")
    parser.add_argument("--customers", help="customers CSV (default: data/customers.csv)")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    conn = build_db(args.db, args.customers)
    for table in ("customers", "orders", "order_items"):
        count = conn.execute(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {table}").fetchone()[0]
        print(f"{table:<12} {count:>4} rows")
    conn.close()
    print(f"Saved {args.db}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

steps.title: Queries 1-3: GROUP BY and joins
steps.body:
customers_per_country is plain GROUP BY. revenue_by_customer uses a LEFT JOIN so customers with no completed orders still appear with 0 (COALESCE turns NULL into 0).

Note the status filter is in the ON clause. Put it in WHERE and those customers vanish, because their NULL status fails the filter. customers_without_orders is an anti-join: LEFT JOIN, then keep rows where the right side is NULL.
steps.code:
-- Each query starts with a "-- name:" line. run_queries.py splits on those lines.
-- Revenue means orders with status = 'completed'.

-- name: customers_per_country
-- GROUP BY basics: how many customers in each country?
SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY customers DESC, country;

-- name: revenue_by_customer
-- LEFT JOIN keeps customers with no completed orders; COALESCE turns NULL into 0.
-- The status filter sits in ON, not WHERE: in WHERE it would silently drop them.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       COUNT(o.order_id)          AS orders,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0)  AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC, c.customer_id;

-- name: customers_without_orders
-- Anti-join: customers with no orders of any status.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.signup_date
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

steps.title: Queries 4-6: window functions
steps.body: A window function computes over related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY does. SUM() OVER (ORDER BY month) gives a running total. RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ...) restarts ranking in each country, so rnk = 1 is the top customer per country. LAG() reads the previous row of the same customer to measure days between orders.
steps.code:
-- name: monthly_revenue_running
-- Window function: running total over months.
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running_total
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

-- name: top_customer_per_country
-- Window function: RANK() restarts for each country (PARTITION BY).
WITH revenue AS (
    SELECT c.country, c.name, SUM(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM customers c
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY c.customer_id
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT country, name, revenue,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk
    FROM revenue
)
SELECT country, name, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY country;

-- name: days_between_orders
-- Window function: LAG() looks at the previous order of the same customer.
WITH ordered AS (
    SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
           LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_date
    FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, prev_date, order_date,
       CAST(julianday(order_date) - julianday(prev_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_since_prev
FROM ordered
WHERE prev_date IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;

steps.title: Queries 7-8: the fan-out bug and its fix
steps.body:
fanout_bug wants revenue and units per customer, so it joins orders to order_items. But order 101 has two item rows, so its 45.00 total appears twice and gets summed twice. Total revenue reads 835 instead of 485, and nothing errors.

fanout_fix first collapses items to one row per order in a CTE, then joins. Rule of thumb: aggregate the 'many' side to the grain of the 'one' side before joining, and never sum a header-level column after joining line-level rows.
steps.code:
-- name: fanout_bug
-- BUG: joining order_items repeats each order once per item row,
-- so the order-level total is summed several times. Revenue is inflated.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       SUM(o.total)  AS revenue,
       SUM(oi.qty)   AS units
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-- name: fanout_fix
-- FIX: aggregate items to one row per order first, then join.
WITH items_per_order AS (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(qty) AS units
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name,
       SUM(o.total)  AS revenue,
       SUM(i.units)  AS units
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o           ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN items_per_order i  ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

steps.title: Write the runner
steps.body: load_queries splits queries.sql on the '-- name:' lines, so SQL stays in a .sql file where editors highlight it. run_query returns column names and rows, and format_table prints them as aligned text. With no arguments it builds a fresh in-memory database and runs all eight queries.
steps.code:
"""run_queries.py: run the named queries in queries.sql and print the results.

Usage:
  python run_queries.py                    # all queries, fresh in-memory database
  python run_queries.py fanout_bug fanout_fix
  python run_queries.py --db shop.db       # use a database built by load_db.py
"""
import argparse
import re
import sqlite3
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from load_db import build_db

QUERIES_FILE = Path(__file__).parent / "queries.sql"
NAME_RE = re.compile(r"^--\s*name:\s*(\w+)\s*$", re.MULTILINE)


def load_queries(path=QUERIES_FILE):
    """Split queries.sql into {name: sql} using the '-- name:' marker lines."""
    text = Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    parts = NAME_RE.split(text)  # [preamble, name1, sql1, name2, sql2, ...]
    return {name: sql.strip() for name, sql in zip(parts[1::2], parts[2::2])}


def run_query(conn, sql):
    cur = conn.execute(sql)
    columns = [d[0] for d in cur.description]
    return columns, cur.fetchall()


def format_table(columns, rows):
    cells = [[str(c) for c in columns]] + [["" if v is None else str(v) for v in r] for r in rows]
    widths = [max(len(row[i]) for row in cells) for i in range(len(columns))]
    lines = ["  ".join(v.ljust(w) for v, w in zip(row, widths)) for row in cells]
    lines.insert(1, "  ".join("-" * w for w in widths))
    return "\n".join(lines)


def main(argv=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Run analysis queries.")
    parser.add_argument("names", nargs="*", help="query names to run (default: all)")
    parser.add_argument("--db", help="existing SQLite file (default: build in memory)")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    queries = load_queries()
    unknown = [n for n in args.names if n not in queries]
    if unknown:
        parser.error(f"unknown query: {', '.join(unknown)}. Choose from: {', '.join(queries)}")

    conn = sqlite3.connect(args.db) if args.db else build_db()
    for name in args.names or queries:
        columns, rows = run_query(conn, queries[name])
        print(f"== {name} ({len(rows)} rows)")
        print(format_table(columns, rows))
        print()
    conn.close()
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

steps.title: Assert exact results

project.interview: I loaded cleaned customer data and orders into SQLite and wrote eight analysis queries covering joins, aggregation and window functions, each tested against exact expected results. The story I tell is the fan-out bug: joining line items to orders repeated the order total per line and inflated revenue from 485 to 835 with no error. I fixed it by aggregating to the order grain first, and I would mention trade-offs like SQLite for speed of setup versus Postgres for concurrency, and REAL versus integer cents for money.

ideas: Know the grain of every table (one row per what?) before you join
Aggregate the many side down to the grain of the one side before joining, or sums inflate silently
Window functions add running totals, ranks and previous-row values without collapsing rows
Small fixed datasets let you assert exact query results, which turns SQL into testable code
traps: Summing a header-level column like orders.total after joining line-level rows (fan-out)
Filtering the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE, which quietly turns it into an inner join
Assuming SQLite enforces foreign keys by default; it does not until PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
qa: Revenue on your dashboard is higher than finance's number. How do you debug it?

First check grain: count rows before and after each join. If a join to a one-to-many table like order items multiplies the order rows, any order-level sum is inflated. Compare against a simple trusted query on the orders table alone, then fix by pre-aggregating the many side in a CTE and add a test that the two numbers match.
When would you use a window function instead of GROUP BY?

When you need a per-row result that depends on other rows but still want to keep every row, such as a running total, a rank within a group, or the gap since the previous order. GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group; a window function keeps them and adds a computed column.
